data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The fetch budget must be denominated in both requests and bytes, with exhaustion recorded as a typed terminal state containing the exhausted resource type, remaining budget of the other, and a timestamp.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If all fetch operations are guaranteed to have uniform response sizes and identical request overhead, then a single denomination (requests or bytes) would suffice without loss of reproducibility.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the environment provides only one type of constraint (e.g., API rate limits but no data caps), then the dual budget is unnecessarily complex.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the agent's fetch strategy can dynamically adapt to avoid exhaustion of one resource while the other is still plentiful, then a composite cost function might be more efficient.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The agent maintains two monotonic counters: requests_sent and bytes_received. Before each fetch, it checks if either counter would exceed its limit. If so, it transitions to a terminal state, recording a typed event with fields: exhausted_resource (enum: requests, bytes), limit_value, current_value, timestamp, and the other resource's remaining budget. This event is written to an audit log. The terminal state is a specific state in the agent's state machine, ensuring replayability because the same budget limits and same sequence of fetches will deterministically lead to the same exhaustion point.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
